lessons.title: Sector Rotation in Practice: What Nifty Sector Indices Show Across Past Cycles

body.text: Leadership changes hands almost every year, and the gap between the best and worst sector is usually far bigger than the market's own return. Rotation is real. The problem is that it is only obvious in hindsight, which is why chasing last year's winner is one of the most reliable ways to lose money.

children.text: Chapter 1 sketched how an upcycle travels through the spectrum, from rate cuts to early cyclicals to capital goods to commodities. This lesson tests that story against what Nifty sector indices actually did, year by year. The pattern holds in broad strokes. What the data also shows is how violently leadership reverses, and how little last year's ranking tells you about next year's.

body.caption: Calendar-year price returns of selected Nifty sector indices (%). 2026 is year to date, to 9 September

children.text: Read down the Pharma column first. It lost money in four consecutive years, 2016 through 2019, as US generic price erosion and USFDA problems hit earnings, exactly the company-specific shocks Chapter 3 described. Investors gave up on it. Then in 2020 it returned 60.6%, the best of this group. Now read the IT column: 54.9% in 2020 and 59.6% in 2021, followed by -26.0% in 2022 and further falls in 2025 and 2026. No sector stays on top, and none stays at the bottom.

The clearest rotation in recent Indian market history came either side of 2022, when inflation surged and central banks began raising rates. Adding the Metal and FMCG indices for those years shows the whole spectrum turning at once.

In 2021, the deep cyclical led: Nifty Metal returned 69.7% as global commodity prices surged, while defensive FMCG managed 10.0%. In 2022, the picture inverted for the long-duration winners. IT, which had been priced for permanent growth, fell 26.0% as bond yields rose, while FMCG returned 17.5% and Bank 21.2%. Metal still rose 21.8% for the year, even though it had fallen sharply mid-year, a reminder that calendar years hide a lot.

body.text: Three cautions about tables like this. These are price indices, so they exclude dividends, which matters most for high-payout defensives. Index constituents and weights change over time, so a sector index is not a fixed basket. And a calendar year is an arbitrary window: Nifty Metal ended 2022 up 21.8% despite falling about 28% from its October 2021 high to its June 2022 low, as Chapter 3 showed.

children.text: The Trap: Buying Last Year's Winner

Sectoral fund flows in India reliably chase performance. Money arrives after a sector has run, which means investors systematically buy near the end of a leadership phase. The data shows what that costs. An investor who put money into an IT index fund at the end of 2021, after two spectacular years, was down 26.0% in 2022. An investor who gave up on pharma at the end of 2019, after four consecutive losing years, missed a 60.6% year.

body.title: Two Years in IT
body.prompt: You invest ₹1,00,000 in a Nifty IT index fund at the end of 2020. The index returns 59.6% in 2021 and then -26.0% in 2022. Ignoring costs and dividends, what is your total return over the two years, in percent? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 1.596 × 0.74 = 1.181, so ₹1,00,000 becomes about ₹1,18,100, a two-year gain of 18.1%. Positive, but the investor who arrived at the end of 2021, after seeing that 59.6%, simply took the -26.0%. Same index, completely different experience, decided by entry timing.

body.title: What Does Last Year Tell You?
body.question: Looking at the 12 years in the table, what is the most defensible conclusion about using last year's best-performing sector to pick this year's?
options: Winners persist, so buying last year's leader is a sound strategy
Leadership changes frequently and reverses sharply, so last year's ranking is a poor guide on its own
The worst sector always becomes the best the following year
Sector returns are random, so the economic cycle is irrelevant
body.explanation: IT followed +59.6% with -26.0%, and pharma followed four losing years with +60.6%. Leadership rotates with the cycle, so last year's ranking alone is not predictive. That does not make returns random: the rotation follows rates, inflation, and earnings cycles, which is why the tools from Chapters 4 and 5 matter more than the leaderboard.

columns.label: Fixed allocation with rebalancing
points: Decide a cyclical and defensive mix in advance and hold it
Rebalance on a schedule, which mechanically trims winners and adds to laggards
Needs no forecast of the cycle
Captures some rotation benefit without timing risk

columns.label: Deliberate tilting
points: Shift weights gradually based on indicators, rates, and valuations
Requires evidence from Chapter 5 indicators, not headlines
Works best when a group is cheap on mid-cycle earnings and conditions are improving
Risk: being early, or mistaking a structural decline for a cyclical dip

children.text: The third way is the one most investors should consider first: do nothing at the sector level. A diversified fund or index already holds every one of these sectors, and its own weights shift as sectors grow and shrink. Sector rotation then happens inside your portfolio without you making a single call.

body.title: The Sectoral Fund Decision
body.scenario: Ravi, an experienced retail investor, has held a diversified flexi-cap fund for years. A pharma fund has been the top performer in his fund house's list for the last two years, and a friend says healthcare is defensive and will keep winning. Ravi is considering moving 40% of his equity portfolio into it. He has not looked at pharma valuations or at what drove the last two years of returns.
body.prompt: Walk Ravi through how to think about this, using the rotation evidence and the tools from earlier chapters.
body.modelAnswer: Start with the pattern: pharma lost money in four straight years to 2019 and then delivered 60.6% in 2020, and sector leadership in this table reverses often, so two strong years are not evidence that a third is coming. Next, ask what drove the gains: if earnings grew, the rerating may be justified, but if the multiple expanded faster than earnings, Chapter 4's warning about paying up applies. Then check the risk he is actually buying: Chapter 3 showed that pharma is quasi-defensive, with US pricing, USFDA inspections, and the rupee driving earnings more than Indian GDP, so it is not the same as staples defensiveness. Finally, consider concentration: 40% of his equity in one sector removes much of the diversification his flexi-cap fund gives him, and his fund probably already holds pharma. A smaller tilt, sized so a bad sector year does not derail his plan, is more sensible than a 40% switch made after the returns have happened.

body.title: The Rebalancing Effect
body.textWithBlank: Rebalancing back to a fixed cyclical and defensive mix mechanically forces you to trim the ___ and add to the laggards, which is the opposite of chasing performance.
body.explanation: Because rebalancing sells what has risen above its target weight and buys what has fallen below it, it captures part of the rotation benefit without requiring any forecast.

body.title: Before Acting on a Rotation View
steps: Write down which phase of the cycle you think you are in, and the indicator evidence behind it
Check whether the sector is cheap or expensive on mid-cycle earnings, not current earnings
Look at the last three years of sector returns and ask whether you are arriving late
Check what your existing diversified funds already hold in that sector
Size any tilt so that being wrong costs you a tolerable amount
Decide in advance what would tell you the view is wrong, and when you would reverse it
Set a rebalancing schedule so the decision is not left to how you feel after a big move

points: Sector leadership rotates with the cycle, and the gap between the best and worst sector averaged roughly 36 percentage points a year across these indices
Nifty Pharma lost money in four straight years to 2019 and then returned 60.6% in 2020; Nifty IT gained 59.6% in 2021 and lost 26.0% in 2022
The 2022 reversal fits the rate cycle: banks and defensives with pricing power led while expensive long-duration growth derated
Calendar-year tables hide large moves within the year, exclude dividends, and rest on changing index constituents
Chasing last year's winning sector means buying near the end of a leadership phase
For most investors, a fixed cyclical and defensive mix with regular rebalancing captures rotation without requiring forecasts

body.text: Returns are calculated from daily closing levels of Nifty sector price indices compiled from historical market data and rounded to one decimal place; they exclude dividends. The 2026 figure covers 1 January to 9 September 2026 and is not a full year. Metal and FMCG figures are shown only for 2020 to 2022, the period covered by the data used here. Verify against official NSE Indices data before relying on any figure. Ravi's scenario is illustrative. Past performance does not indicate future results, and this lesson is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security or fund.
